resources.title: Spruce grouse
resources.description: Identify spruce grouse by sex and region, understand their conifer-forest habitat, and avoid confusion with ruffed grouse.
resources.quickAnswer: Spruce grouse (Canachites canadensis): Crow-sized grouse. Male: gray with a white-edged black throat and chest, red combs above the eyes and a black tail tipped rusty (except the Franklin's form). This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Habitat
keyFacts.value: Dense younger spruce, fir and pine forest

rangeSummary.value: Across Alaska and the boreal forest of Canada, south into the Rockies, Great Lakes states and northern New England.

identification.text: Crow-sized grouse.
Male: gray with a white-edged black throat and chest, red combs above the eyes and a black tail tipped rusty (except the Franklin's form).
Female: reddish or grayish with a shorter, darker tail than the ruffed grouse and black-and-white barring on the belly.
Compared with the ruffed grouse: Ruffed grouse have a longer tail, longer broader side bars and lack belly barring.

habitat.text: Dense conifer forest of spruce, pine, fir or hemlock with undergrowth; also regenerating jack pine burns.

seasonalBehavior.text: Conifer needles supply most of the diet for much of the year; birds also forage on the ground for fresh growth, berries and insects.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt for current location- and date-specific rules. This biological profile does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Notoriously tame and easy to overlook.
Males give a very low krrrk and drum with the wings.
Feeds on the ground in summer and almost entirely in trees in winter, eating conifer needles.
Mostly permanent resident; some females walk short distances between seasonal territories.

resources.title: Sharp-tailed grouse
resources.description: Identify sharp-tailed grouse by their pointed tail, V-shaped belly marks and grassland-to-boreal habitat.
resources.quickAnswer: Sharp-tailed grouse (Tympanuchus phasianellus): Underparts mostly spotted rather than barred. In flight shows a longer tail with white outer feathers. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Key field mark
keyFacts.value: Pointed central tail feathers and V-shaped belly marks

rangeSummary.value: Resident locally from Alaska and Yukon east to western Quebec and south to eastern Washington, Idaho, Utah, Colorado, Nebraska, the Dakotas, Minnesota, Wisconsin and northern Michigan; it has disappeared from parts of its former southern range.

identification.text: Underparts mostly spotted rather than barred.
In flight shows a longer tail with white outer feathers.
Sexes similar; male slightly larger (38–53 cm).
Compared with the greater and lesser prairie-chickens: Prairie-chickens have barred underparts; the sharp-tail is spotted and has a longer, white-edged tail.

habitat.text: Open prairie mixed with groves of aspen, birch, willow or shrubs, forest edges and open burns in coniferous forest; more open grassland in summer, groves in winter.

seasonalBehavior.text: Males gather on traditional display grounds called leks in spring; outside display periods birds forage on the ground and in shrubs or trees.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt for current rules. A species occurrence or profile is not a legal hunting determination.

behavior.text: Displays on leks; seasonal home ranges are usually within about 2 km of the lek
May roost at night by burrowing into snowdrifts
Forages on the ground in summer and in trees and shrubs in winter, when it eats buds; takes grasshoppers and other insects in summer

resources.title: Wild turkey
resources.description: Identify wild turkey, recognize sex and regional variation, and understand its forest-edge habitat and roosting behaviour.
resources.quickAnswer: Wild turkey (Meleagris gallopavo): Huge ground bird, 1.1-1.2 m long, with a naked head and a long, wide tail. Trimmer and stronger-looking than the domestic barnyard turkey. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Habitat
keyFacts.value: Mature forest interspersed with fields, clearings and edges

rangeSummary.value: Native to North America; depleted by 1900 but reintroduced to most of its former range and established in new areas, now found across the United States and in southern Western and Eastern Canada, and adapting to suburban edges in the East.

identification.text: Huge ground bird, 1.1-1.2 m long, with a naked head and a long, wide tail.
Trimmer and stronger-looking than the domestic barnyard turkey.
Females and young are smaller and duller than adult males.

habitat.text: Varies across the continent: oak-hickory and pine-oak forests, cypress swamps, mesquite grassland, pinyon-juniper and chaparral, usually near oaks. Best habitat mixes woodland and open clearings.

seasonalBehavior.text: Turkeys scratch leaf litter while foraging, form flocks, and fly into trees to roost at night. Males perform strutting courtship displays in spring.

huntingContext.text: Sex, age, licence, tag, method, place and date can all matter. Check Hunt and the responsible authority; this page does not establish legality.

sexDifferences.text: Adult males are generally larger and more iridescent, with more prominent head and neck ornamentation; beard presence alone must not be equated automatically with male sex.

ageDifferences.text: Juvenile plumage and proportions differ from adults; jake is hunter terminology for a young male, not a separate species.

behavior.text: Males gobble in spring and strut with feathers puffed, tail fanned, wattles swollen and wings drooped; one male mates with several females.
Usually walks or runs but flies strongly; roosts overnight in tall trees.
Forages on the ground, scratching leaf litter, most actively in early morning and evening; acorns are a favourite food.
Not migratory, but may wander, especially in fall.

resources.title: White-tailed deer
resources.description: Identify white-tailed deer, understand their broad Ontario habitat and distinguish biological presence from hunting legality.
resources.quickAnswer: White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) are medium-to-large cervids named for the bright underside of the tail, often raised when alarmed. In Ontario they occupy landscapes from the southern agricultural belt into the boreal forest, but occurrence does not establish an open season.

keyFacts.label: Ontario context
keyFacts.value: From the southern agricultural belt into boreal forest

rangeSummary.value: Widely distributed in North America; Ontario range and density shift with winter severity, climate and habitat.

identification.text: Confirm the white underside of the tail and the animal's overall proportions. Antlers are not a universal identity cue because females and young lack them and males shed them seasonally.

habitat.text: Ontario deer use forest, edge and agricultural landscapes. Winter severity strongly affects population growth and northern range, so broad range should not be read as exact local presence.

seasonalBehavior.text: Some deer concentrate in suitable winter woodlands; the importance and composition of these areas vary by ecoregion and snow conditions.

huntingContext.text: Use Hunt for place-, date- and method-specific rules. Biological range does not establish huntability, season status or tag requirements.

sexDifferences.text: Adult bucks usually carry antlers during part of the year; antler presence is seasonal and cannot be treated as a permanent definition of biological sex.

ageDifferences.text: Fawns are young deer, often spotted early in life. Regulatory age or antler-class definitions must come from the applicable rule.

behavior.text: Rut peaks in the last three weeks of November in Canada; bucks' necks swell and they travel almost constantly.
Gathers in winter 'deer yards' for food and shelter from deep snow.
Eats leafy plants, grasses, mushrooms and berries in summer; twigs, buds, acorns and waste grain in fall and winter.
Does leave nearly scentless spotted fawns hidden for hours.

conservationStatus.text: Columbian white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus leucurus), Columbia River (Clark, Cowliz, Pacific, Skamania, and Wahkiakum Counties, WA., and Clatsop, Columbia, and Multnomah Counties, OR.): listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 1967-03-11.
Key deer (Odocoileus virginianus clavium): listed as endangered under the Endangered Species Act since 1967-03-11.

resources.title: Moose
resources.description: Identify moose, understand seasonal habitat needs and avoid treating broad range as a hunting-rule answer.
resources.quickAnswer: Moose (Alces alces): Largest deer; up to almost 1.8 m at the shoulder, with a humped shoulder and low rump. Long mournful arched nose with a flexible upper lip; most have a fur-covered 'bell' hanging from the throat. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Habitat pattern
keyFacts.value: A mixture of young browse, mature shelter, aquatic feeding sites and localized features

rangeSummary.value: Across the northern forests of North America from Alaska and Canada south into the Rocky Mountains and the northern United States; introduced to Newfoundland and Colorado.

identification.text: Largest deer; up to almost 1.8 m at the shoulder, with a humped shoulder and low rump.
Long mournful arched nose with a flexible upper lip; most have a fur-covered 'bell' hanging from the throat.
Dark brown to nearly black, reddish or grayish brown with pale gray or white leg 'stockings'.
Only bulls carry antlers: broad palms fringed with spikes, grown each summer.
Newborn calves are red-brown.

habitat.text: A mosaic of second-growth forest, openings, swamps, lakes and wetlands; needs water for summer foraging and hardwood-conifer forest for winter cover; recent burns with dense willow, aspen and birch are prime.

seasonalBehavior.text: Moose move among habitat types with season. Mature cover helps shelter them from extreme summer and winter weather, while disturbance can create nutritious young browse.

huntingContext.text: Cow, calf and bull classifications, allocations and rules can vary by place and date. Confirm the animal and use current regulatory sources; this profile cannot authorize a hunt.

sexDifferences.text: Adult bulls may carry broad antlers; cows do not, but a bull can be antlerless after shedding.

ageDifferences.text: A biological calf is a young moose. Any legally defined calf criterion belongs to the applicable regulation.

behavior.text: Rut in late September–early October; cows bawl nasally and bulls answer with a coughing bellow
Browses willow, birch and aspen twigs in fall and winter, sometimes leaving a browse line 1.8–2.4 m high; feeds on aquatic plants in summer
Makes seasonal movements of a few to about 100 km between calving, rutting and wintering areas
Cools off in water in summer and may dive for bottom plants

resources.title: American black bear
resources.description: Identify American black bear, understand colour variation and forest habitat, and keep safety separate from hunting rules.
resources.quickAnswer: American black bear (Ursus americanus): Usually black, especially in eastern North America; western animals are often brown, cinnamon or blonde, and some coastal British Columbia and Alaska bears are creamy white or bluish-grey. Pale muzzle contrasting with darker fur; sometimes a white chest spot. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Colour variation
keyFacts.value: Black, cinnamon or brown in Ontario

rangeSummary.value: From northern Alaska east across virtually all of Canada to Labrador and Newfoundland, and south through much of the United States into central Mexico.

identification.text: Usually black, especially in eastern North America; western animals are often brown, cinnamon or blonde, and some coastal British Columbia and Alaska bears are creamy white or bluish-grey.
Pale muzzle contrasting with darker fur; sometimes a white chest spot.
Compared with grizzly/brown bears: longer, less heavily furred ears, a smaller shoulder hump and a convex rather than concave (dished) facial profile.
Males larger: males 47-409 kg, females 39-236 kg.

Compared with the grizzly (brown) bear: The grizzly has a larger shoulder hump, shorter, furrier ears and a concave (dished) profile; colour alone is unreliable because black bears can be brown, cinnamon or blonde.

habitat.text: Prime habitat is relatively inaccessible terrain with thick understorey and abundant fruit or nut crops: hardwood-conifer forest in the Northeast, oak-hickory and swampy lowlands in the Southeast, and chaparral and pinyon-juniper at 900-3,000 m in the Southwest.

seasonalBehavior.text: Bears enter dens for winter; timing and behaviour vary with latitude, food, sex and reproductive status. Never infer absence from season alone.

huntingContext.text: Identification, safety and legality are separate questions. Use Hunt and the responsible authority for current rules, and follow bear-safety guidance during any encounter.

behavior.text: Generally active at dawn and dusk; near human food it may become daytime-active (roadsides) or nocturnal (campgrounds).
Mostly solitary except females with cubs, summer breeding pairs and gatherings at concentrated food sources.
Diet is mostly plant: grasses and forbs in spring, soft fruit in summer, and hard and soft mast in fall; animal food is mainly colonial insects and carrion.
Spends winter in dens; cubs are born in January-February while the female is dormant.

resources.title: Snowshoe hare
resources.description: Identify snowshoe hare across seasonal coat changes and distinguish it from rabbits and Arctic hare.
resources.quickAnswer: Snowshoe hare (Lepus americanus) is a forest hare with large, heavily furred hind feet and black-tipped ears. Most populations change from brown in warmer months to white in winter, so coat colour alone is unreliable during transition.

keyFacts.label: Key field marks
keyFacts.value: Large hind feet and black-tipped ears

rangeSummary.value: Forested Canada, Alaska and the northern United States, extending south in some mountain regions.

identification.text: Large, furred hind feet and black-tipped ears matter throughout the year. The coat changes from brown to white seasonally; Arctic hare is larger and has more distinct black ear tips in overlap areas.

habitat.text: Snowshoe hare is a forest species that uses dense conifer, riparian woodland, willow-birch scrub and other habitats with protective understory cover.

seasonalBehavior.text: The coat molts brown in spring and white in fall. Summer foods include succulent vegetation; winter foods shift toward twigs, buds and bark.

signsAndTracks.text: The oversized hind feet leave a characteristic paired print ahead of the smaller forefeet when the hare bounds; well-used winter trails can be conspicuous in snow.

huntingContext.text: Do not convert tracks, range or species identity into a legal answer. Use Hunt and current official sources for the location and date.

behavior.text: Most active from sundown to dawn and active all winter; rests by day in sheltered 'forms' under bushes, stumps or logs.
Keeps a network of well-maintained runways that follow the same routes summer and winter and become conspicuous after snowfall.
Eats herbaceous plants and shrub leaves in summer; twigs, buds and bark of conifers, aspen and willow in winter.
Populations cycle between high abundance and scarcity; generally silent but snorts, and clicks during breeding season.

resources.title: Mallard
resources.description: Identify mallards across sex and seasonal plumage, including the wing speculum and black-duck confusion risk.
resources.quickAnswer: Mallard (Anas platyrhynchos): Drake: glossy green head, yellow bill, white neck ring, chestnut breast, gray body and curled black tail feathers. Hen: mottled brown with an orange bill marked with black, and orange legs. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Shared field mark
keyFacts.value: Blue speculum bordered by white bars

rangeSummary.value: Across Alaska, Canada (most numerous in the Prairie Provinces, expanding eastward) and most of the US; winters in southern Ontario and British Columbia and farther south. Also native to Europe and Asia.

identification.text: Drake: glossy green head, yellow bill, white neck ring, chestnut breast, gray body and curled black tail feathers.
Hen: mottled brown with an orange bill marked with black, and orange legs.
Both sexes show a blue to purplish-blue speculum bordered in white.
Compared with the american black duck: Black ducks are much darker with a gray head and a speculum lacking bold white borders.
Compared with the mottled duck: Compare female mallards with mottled ducks in Florida and on the Gulf Coast.
Compared with the mexican duck: Compare female mallards with Mexican ducks in the Southwest.

habitat.text: Marshes, prairie potholes and reed-ringed sloughs, ponds, rivers, lakes, bays, grain fields and city parks; prefers fresh water.

seasonalBehavior.text: Males enter brown eclipse plumage after breeding and can resemble females. Mallards also hybridize with American black ducks, creating intermediate-looking birds.

huntingContext.text: Waterfowl identification can affect species-specific limits. Confirm identification before relying on Hunt regulations; this page does not establish an open season.

behavior.text: Dabbles, up-ends with tail vertical, occasionally dives, and grazes on land.
Eats mostly plant material (seeds, roots, pondweeds, acorns, grain) plus insects, crustaceans and mollusks.
Hen gives the familiar loud quack; drake gives softer, reedy calls.
Readily attracted by decoys; pairs form in fall and winter.

resources.title: Canada goose
resources.description: Identify Canada goose and distinguish it from cackling goose using structure, size and regional context.
resources.quickAnswer: Canada goose (Branta canadensis): White chinstrap on a black head and neck. Large: 76 cm–1.2 m long, 2.9–8.9 kg. This profile does not establish whether taking it is legal anywhere.

keyFacts.label: Key field marks
keyFacts.value: Long black neck, white cheek patch and smoothly sloping bill-to-forehead profile

rangeSummary.value: Breeds from central and southeastern Alaska across northern Canada south to southwestern British Columbia and much of the northern and central United States; resident year-round in the central part of the range, with many populations in urban areas no longer migrating.

identification.text: White chinstrap on a black head and neck.
Large: 76 cm–1.2 m long, 2.9–8.9 kg.
Populations vary greatly in size and body colour, from white-chested to very dark.
Sexes alike; male slightly larger.
Compared with the cackling goose: The smallest forms formerly included in this species are now treated as the separate Cackling Goose; compare size closely.

habitat.text: Always nests near water: tundra, fresh and salt marshes, wooded lakes, and city park and suburban ponds; winters where fields for feeding are within commuting distance of water.

seasonalBehavior.text: Pairs and flocks move between water and feeding areas; some populations migrate while others remain resident. Location and date affect which population is present.

huntingContext.text: Canada and cackling goose rules can be combined or species-specific by district. Confirm the bird before relying on regulations; this profile is not a legal determination.

behavior.text: Flies in V-formation, northbound in spring and southbound in fall; family groups migrate together
Grazes mostly while walking on land; also feeds in water by dipping or up-ending
Many urban and refuge birds are now permanent residents
Feeds in flocks at most seasons, often in open fields in winter

content.plainText: Spruce grouse plumage varies by sex and regional form. Compare the whole bird—tail pattern, barring, breast and habitat—and do not substitute a generic “grouse” identification.
Focus on relatively dense younger spruce, fir or pine forest, including regenerating tracts and bog edges; conifer needles form the core food supply.
Confirm the pointed central tail feathers and V-shaped belly marks. Northern birds can be substantially darker than prairie birds.
Sex and age may matter in regulations. Do not use a displaying adult male as the visual template for every turkey; females and young differ markedly.
Antlers are seasonal and do not identify every white-tailed deer. Confirm tail, proportions and local cervid lookalikes before relying on any sex- or age-specific rule.
Confirm cow, calf or bull using more than antler presence. Tag and season classifications are regulatory facts and must come from the current authority.
Black-bear coat colour ranges from black to cinnamon or brown. Colour alone cannot establish species where other bears overlap; use authoritative regional comparison guidance.
Coat colour changes seasonally. Use the large furred hind feet and black-tipped ears, and distinguish snowshoe hare from Arctic hare or local rabbits.
Female, juvenile and eclipse-plumage mallards are not green-headed. Confirm bill, body pattern and white-bordered blue speculum, and account for American black duck hybrids.
Cackling goose shares the black head and white cheek patch. Compare overall size, neck length, bill and head shape before relying on species-specific rules.
